chapter_text:
CHAPTER 15 - LIGHT ENERGY

Introduction

Light is a form of energy that enables us to see the world around us. It travels in straight lines in a uniform medium and moves extremely fast - about 3 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum. When light meets a surface or passes from one medium to another, it bends, bounces or splits in predictable ways. This chapter studies the main behaviours of light: reflection (by mirrors), refraction (by lenses and slabs), how the human eye forms images and how its defects are corrected, and the dispersion and scattering of light that paint the sky and the rainbow.

15.1 NATURE OF LIGHT AND RECTILINEAR PROPAGATION

Light is electromagnetic radiation that the eye can detect (visible light, wavelength roughly 400 nm to 700 nm). In a single uniform medium, light travels in straight lines - this is called RECTILINEAR PROPAGATION. The formation of sharp shadows and the working of a pinhole camera are evidence of this. A ray is the straight-line path of light; a beam is a bundle of rays.

15.2 REFLECTION OF LIGHT

When light falls on a surface and bounces back into the same medium, the process is called REFLECTION. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal (the perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence) all play a role. The angle of incidence (i) is measured between the incident ray and the normal; the angle of reflection (r) is between the reflected ray and the normal.

Laws of reflection:
 1. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (i = r).
 2. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane.
These laws hold for every reflecting surface - flat or curved.

15.3 PLANE MIRRORS

A plane mirror is a flat reflecting surface. The image formed by a plane mirror is:
 - VIRTUAL (cannot be caught on a screen) and ERECT (upright);
 - the same SIZE as the object;
 - as far BEHIND the mirror as the object is in front;
 - laterally inverted (left and right appear swapped).
Lateral inversion is why the word AMBULANCE is written mirror-reversed on the front of the vehicle.

15.4 SPHERICAL MIRRORS

A spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere whose one side is silvered. If the reflecting surface is the inner (caved-in) side, it is a CONCAVE mirror; if it is the outer (bulging) side, it is a CONVEX mirror.

Key terms:
 - POLE (P): the centre of the mirror's reflecting surface.
 - CENTRE OF CURVATURE (C): the centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part.
 - RADIUS OF CURVATURE (R): the radius of that sphere; the distance PC.
 - PRINCIPAL AXIS: the straight line through P and C.
 - PRINCIPAL FOCUS (F): the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis meet (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex) after reflection.
 - FOCAL LENGTH (f): the distance PF.
For a spherical mirror the focus lies midway between the pole and the centre of curvature, so
   f = R / 2.

15.5 IMAGE FORMATION BY SPHERICAL MIRRORS

For a CONCAVE mirror, as the object moves from far away towards the mirror, the image changes:
 - Object at infinity: image at F, real, inverted, highly diminished (point image).
 - Object beyond C: image between F and C, real, inverted, diminished.
 - Object at C: image at C, real, inverted, same size.
 - Object between C and F: image beyond C, real, inverted, enlarged.
 - Object at F: image at infinity, real, inverted, highly enlarged.
 - Object between F and P: image behind the mirror, virtual, erect, enlarged.
A CONVEX mirror always forms a VIRTUAL, ERECT and DIMINISHED image, located between the pole and the focus behind the mirror, for every position of the object.

15.6 MIRROR FORMULA AND MAGNIFICATION

The mirror formula relates object distance u, image distance v and focal length f:
   1/v + 1/u = 1/f
Linear magnification m is the ratio of image height h' to object height h, and also equals -v/u:
   m = h'/h = -v/u
A negative m means a real, inverted image; a positive m means a virtual, erect image.

NEW CARTESIAN SIGN CONVENTION:
 - All distances are measured from the pole.
 - Distances measured in the direction of the incident light (to the right) are POSITIVE; those against it (to the left) are NEGATIVE.
 - Heights measured upward (above the axis) are positive; downward, negative.
Consequences: for a concave mirror f and R are negative; for a convex mirror f and R are positive. The object distance u is always negative (object is in front of the mirror).

15.7 USES OF SPHERICAL MIRRORS

Concave mirrors are used as shaving/make-up mirrors (enlarged erect image when the face is within the focus), as reflectors in torches, headlights and search-lights (source at focus gives a parallel beam), in solar cookers and solar furnaces (to concentrate sunlight), and by dentists and ENT doctors. Convex mirrors are used as rear-view (wing) mirrors in vehicles and as security mirrors, because they always give an erect, diminished image and a wide field of view.

15.8 REFRACTION OF LIGHT

When light passes from one transparent medium into another, its speed changes and it bends. This bending is called REFRACTION. A ray going from a rarer medium (e.g. air) into a denser medium (e.g. glass) bends TOWARDS the normal; going from denser to rarer, it bends AWAY from the normal. A ray hitting the surface along the normal (i = 0) passes straight through without bending.

Laws of refraction:
 1. The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal lie in the same plane.
 2. Snell's law: the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant for a given pair of media: sin i / sin r = constant = n (the refractive index).

REFRACTIVE INDEX: The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum (c) to its speed in the medium (v):
   n = c / v
Because v is always less than c, n is always greater than 1. A higher n means a denser (more optically resistant) medium and more bending. For water n is about 1.33; for ordinary glass about 1.5; for diamond about 2.42.

15.9 REFRACTION THROUGH A GLASS SLAB

When light passes through a rectangular glass slab, it bends towards the normal on entering and away from the normal on leaving. Because the two faces are parallel, the emergent ray is PARALLEL to the incident ray but is shifted sideways. This sideways shift is the LATERAL DISPLACEMENT. The net deviation of the ray's direction is zero, but it emerges along a different (parallel) line.

15.10 LENSES

A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one of which is curved. A CONVEX (converging) lens is thicker at the middle and bends parallel rays to meet at a real focus. A CONCAVE (diverging) lens is thinner at the middle and spreads parallel rays so that they appear to diverge from a virtual focus. The OPTICAL CENTRE is the central point through which a ray passes undeviated; the PRINCIPAL FOCUS is where parallel rays converge (or appear to diverge from); the FOCAL LENGTH f is the distance from the optical centre to the principal focus.

Image formation by a CONVEX lens (object moving in from infinity) mirrors the concave-mirror sequence: real inverted images that shrink, equal, then enlarge as the object approaches 2F and F, and a virtual erect enlarged image when the object is within the focus (the magnifying-glass case). A CONCAVE lens always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image between the optical centre and the focus.

15.11 LENS FORMULA, MAGNIFICATION AND POWER

The lens formula relates object distance u, image distance v and focal length f:
   1/v - 1/u = 1/f
Magnification for a lens:
   m = h'/h = v/u
Sign convention is the same New Cartesian rule: a convex lens has positive f, a concave lens negative f.

POWER OF A LENS: The power P measures how strongly a lens converges or diverges light. It is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres:
   P = 1 / f (with f in metres)
The unit of power is the DIOPTRE (D); 1 D = 1 per metre. A convex lens has positive power; a concave lens has negative power. When thin lenses are placed in contact, their powers add: P = P1 + P2 + ...

15.12 THE HUMAN EYE

The human eye is a natural optical instrument that works like a camera. Its main parts:
 - CORNEA: the transparent front layer where most of the bending of light happens.
 - IRIS: the coloured ring that controls the size of the pupil.
 - PUPIL: the central opening that lets light in; it widens in dim light and narrows in bright light.
 - EYE LENS: a flexible convex lens that fine-tunes the focus by changing its shape (ACCOMMODATION), controlled by the ciliary muscles.
 - RETINA: the light-sensitive screen at the back where a real, inverted, diminished image forms; it contains rods and cones.
 - OPTIC NERVE: carries the signal to the brain, which interprets the image as upright.
The least distance of distinct vision for a normal eye is about 25 cm; the far point is infinity.

15.13 DEFECTS OF VISION AND THEIR CORRECTION

MYOPIA (short-sightedness): a person can see nearby objects clearly but distant objects appear blurred. The image of a distant object forms IN FRONT of the retina because the eyeball is too long or the lens is too converging. Correction: a CONCAVE (diverging) lens of suitable power, which spreads the rays so the image falls back on the retina.

HYPERMETROPIA (long-sightedness): a person can see distant objects clearly but nearby objects appear blurred. The image of a near object forms BEHIND the retina because the eyeball is too short or the lens is too weak. Correction: a CONVEX (converging) lens of suitable power.

PRESBYOPIA: an age-related defect in which the eye lens loses flexibility and the ciliary muscles weaken, so the near point recedes and accommodation fails. The person struggles with both near and (sometimes) distant vision. Correction: bifocal lenses - a concave portion for distant vision and a convex portion for near vision.

15.14 DISPERSION OF WHITE LIGHT

When a beam of white light passes through a glass prism, it splits into its component colours. This splitting is called DISPERSION. The band of colours produced is the SPECTRUM, in the order:
   Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red - remembered as VIBGYOR.
Dispersion happens because different colours travel at slightly different speeds in glass and so are bent by different amounts: violet (shortest wavelength) bends the most, red (longest wavelength) the least. A rainbow is a natural example - water droplets in the air act as tiny prisms, dispersing sunlight.

15.15 ATMOSPHERIC REFRACTION

The atmosphere is not uniform - air near the ground is denser and warmer than air higher up. Light from distant objects bends as it passes through these layers of varying density - this is ATMOSPHERIC REFRACTION. It causes the TWINKLING of stars (their apparent position shifts as the air fluctuates), and the apparent flattening and early rising / late setting of the Sun (we see the Sun a couple of minutes before it actually rises and after it actually sets).

15.16 SCATTERING OF LIGHT

When light strikes very small particles (molecules, dust, water droplets), it is redirected in all directions - this is SCATTERING. The amount of scattering depends on wavelength: shorter wavelengths (blue) scatter much more than longer ones (red).
 - BLUE SKY: air molecules scatter the blue component of sunlight in all directions, so the sky looks blue.
 - RED SUNRISE AND SUNSET: at sunrise/sunset, sunlight travels a long path through the atmosphere; most of the blue is scattered away, so the Sun and sky near it look red/orange.
 - TYNDALL EFFECT: when light passes through a colloid (e.g. smoke, fog, a dusty room), the path of the beam becomes visible because the colloidal particles scatter the light. This is the Tyndall effect.

15.17 WORKED NUMERICALS

Example 1 (mirror): An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the image distance.
 Using sign convention: u = -30 cm, f = -20 cm. Mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f gives
   1/v = 1/f - 1/u = (1/-20) - (1/-30) = -1/20 + 1/30 = -3/60 + 2/60 = -1/60.
 So v = -60 cm. The image is 60 cm in front of the mirror, real and inverted.
 Magnification m = -v/u = -(-60)/(-30) = -2. The image is twice as tall and inverted.

Example 2 (lens): A convex lens has focal length 25 cm. Find its power.
 f = 25 cm = 0.25 m. P = 1/f = 1/0.25 = +4 D. A converging lens of power +4 dioptres.

Example 3 (refractive index): Light travels at 2 x 10^8 m/s in a medium. Find its refractive index.
 n = c/v = (3 x 10^8) / (2 x 10^8) = 1.5. The medium is like ordinary glass.

SUMMARY

- Light is a form of energy that travels in straight lines and very fast (3 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum).
- Reflection obeys i = r, with the incident ray, reflected ray and normal in one plane. Plane mirrors give virtual, erect, same-size, laterally-inverted images.
- Spherical mirrors: concave (converging) and convex (diverging). f = R/2. Mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; magnification m = -v/u = h'/h. Concave mirrors give varied images; convex mirrors always give virtual, erect, diminished images.
- Refraction bends light at a boundary; n = c/v (>1); Snell's law sin i / sin r = n. A glass slab shifts the ray sideways (lateral displacement) without changing its direction.
- Lenses: convex (converging) and concave (diverging). Lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f; m = v/u; power P = 1/f in dioptres.
- The eye forms a real inverted image on the retina; defects are myopia (concave lens), hypermetropia (convex lens) and presbyopia (bifocals).
- A prism disperses white light into VIBGYOR. Atmospheric refraction makes stars twinkle. Scattering makes the sky blue and the sunrise/sunset red, and produces the Tyndall effect.

topics.name: Reflection and Plane Mirrors
topics.description: Nature of light and rectilinear propagation; reflection of light; the laws of reflection (i = r, rays and normal coplanar); plane mirrors and the properties of the images they form (virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted).

topics.name: Spherical Mirrors and Mirror Formula
topics.description: Concave and convex mirrors; terms - pole, centre of curvature, radius of curvature, principal focus, focal length, f = R/2; image formation; the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, magnification m = -v/u, the sign convention and uses of mirrors.

topics.name: Refraction and Refractive Index
topics.description: Refraction of light, the laws of refraction and Snell's law; refractive index n = c/v; bending towards/away from the normal; refraction through a parallel-sided glass slab and lateral displacement.

topics.name: Lenses and Lens Formula
topics.description: Convex and concave lenses; image formation; the lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, magnification m = v/u; power of a lens P = 1/f measured in dioptres; combination of lenses in contact.

topics.name: Human Eye and Defects of Vision
topics.description: Parts of the human eye and how it focuses (accommodation); the retinal image; defects of vision - myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia - and their correction using concave, convex and bifocal lenses.

topics.name: Dispersion and Scattering of Light
topics.description: Dispersion of white light by a prism (VIBGYOR) and the rainbow; atmospheric refraction (twinkling of stars, early sunrise/late sunset); scattering of light - the blue sky, the red sunrise/sunset and the Tyndall effect.

chapter_summary.title: Light Energy - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) summary for Lesson 15. It covers how light reflects from plane and spherical mirrors, refracts through slabs and lenses, forms images in the human eye, and disperses and scatters in the atmosphere - together with the mirror and lens formulae, magnification and power.

sections.heading: Reflection and plane mirrors
bullets: Light is a form of energy that travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation) at about 3 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum.
Laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (i = r), and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.
A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image of the same size, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
The image in a plane mirror is laterally inverted - left and right appear swapped (e.g. mirror-writing of AMBULANCE).

sections.heading: Spherical mirrors and the mirror formula
bullets: A concave mirror reflects from its inner surface and converges light; a convex mirror reflects from its outer surface and diverges light.
Key terms: pole P, centre of curvature C, radius of curvature R, principal focus F and focal length f, with f = R/2.
Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; magnification m = h'/h = -v/u (negative m = real inverted image; positive = virtual erect).
Concave mirrors give a range of images (real or virtual); a convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image.

sections.heading: Refraction and refractive index
bullets: Refraction is the bending of light when it changes medium because its speed changes; towards the normal entering a denser medium, away when entering a rarer one.
Laws of refraction: incident ray, refracted ray and normal are coplanar; Snell's law sin i / sin r = n is constant for a pair of media.
Refractive index n = c/v is always greater than 1; water ~1.33, glass ~1.5, diamond ~2.42.
A parallel-sided glass slab shifts the ray sideways (lateral displacement) but the emergent ray stays parallel to the incident ray.

sections.heading: Lenses, lens formula and power
bullets: A convex (converging) lens is thicker in the middle; a concave (diverging) lens is thinner in the middle.
Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f; magnification m = h'/h = v/u.
Power of a lens P = 1/f (f in metres), measured in dioptres (D); convex lens power is positive, concave negative.
A convex lens forms real images for distant objects and a virtual enlarged image (magnifying glass) when the object is within the focus; a concave lens always forms a virtual, diminished image.

sections.heading: Human eye, dispersion and scattering
bullets: The eye focuses light with the cornea and a flexible convex lens (accommodation) to form a real, inverted image on the retina; least distance of distinct vision is about 25 cm.
Myopia (distant blur) is corrected with a concave lens; hypermetropia (near blur) with a convex lens; presbyopia (age-related) with bifocal lenses.
A prism disperses white light into the spectrum VIBGYOR; violet bends most, red least; a rainbow is natural dispersion by water droplets.
Scattering of light makes the sky blue and the rising/setting Sun red; the Tyndall effect makes a light beam visible in a colloid; atmospheric refraction makes stars twinkle.

key_takeaways: Reflection obeys i = r; a plane mirror gives a virtual, erect, same-size, laterally-inverted image.
For spherical mirrors f = R/2, the mirror formula is 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and magnification m = -v/u.
Refraction bends light because its speed changes; refractive index n = c/v is always greater than 1.
For lenses the formula is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, magnification m = v/u, and power P = 1/f in dioptres.
The eye forms a real inverted image on the retina; myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia are corrected by concave, convex and bifocal lenses respectively.
A prism disperses white light into VIBGYOR; scattering explains the blue sky and red sunset; atmospheric refraction makes stars twinkle.

glossary.definition: The bouncing back of light into the same medium when it strikes a surface; obeys i = r.
The line drawn perpendicular to a surface at the point where a ray strikes it.
A flat reflecting surface that forms a virtual, erect, same-size, laterally-inverted image.
The apparent left-right swapping of an image in a plane mirror.
A spherical mirror that reflects from its inner (caved-in) surface and converges parallel light to a real focus.
A spherical mirror that reflects from its outer (bulging) surface and diverges light; always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image.
The distance between the pole and the principal focus of a mirror or lens; for a mirror f = R/2.
The relation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f connecting image distance, object distance and focal length of a spherical mirror.
The ratio of image height to object height; m = -v/u for mirrors and m = v/u for lenses.
The bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium into another because its speed changes.
The ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in a medium, n = c/v; always greater than 1.
The relation 1/v - 1/u = 1/f connecting image distance, object distance and focal length of a lens.
The reciprocal of focal length in metres, P = 1/f, measured in dioptres (D); positive for convex, negative for concave.
The splitting of white light into its component colours (VIBGYOR) when it passes through a prism.
The redirection of light by small particles; makes the sky blue and the setting Sun red (Tyndall effect in colloids).

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Light Energy (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) Worksheet-15 for Lesson 15 (Light Energy). Attempt all questions. Use c = 3 x 10^8 m/s and the New Cartesian sign convention where needed.

questions.question: State the two laws of reflection of light.
questions.answer:
Law 1: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection (i = r).
Law 2: The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal to the surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
These laws hold for both plane and curved (spherical) mirrors.

questions.question: List the four properties of the image formed by a plane mirror.
questions.answer:
(1) The image is VIRTUAL (it cannot be caught on a screen) and ERECT (upright).
(2) The image is the SAME SIZE as the object.
(3) The image is as far BEHIND the mirror as the object is in front of it.
(4) The image is LATERALLY INVERTED (left and right are apparently swapped).
questions.explanation: Four standard properties of a plane-mirror image.

questions.question: Define the principal focus and focal length of a concave mirror, and state the relation between focal length and radius of curvature.
questions.answer:
Principal focus (F): the point on the principal axis where rays travelling parallel to the axis actually meet after reflection from a concave mirror.
Focal length (f): the distance between the pole (P) and the principal focus (F).
Relation: the focus lies midway between the pole and the centre of curvature, so f = R/2, where R is the radius of curvature.

questions.question: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the position, nature and magnification of the image.
questions.answer:
Given (sign convention): u = -15 cm, f = -10 cm.
Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f.
1/v = 1/f - 1/u = (1/-10) - (1/-15) = -1/10 + 1/15.
LCM 30: = -3/30 + 2/30 = -1/30, so v = -30 cm.
The image is 30 cm in front of the mirror - REAL and INVERTED.
Magnification m = -v/u = -(-30)/(-15) = -2.
The image is twice the size of the object (enlarged) and inverted (m is negative). This matches the rule: object between C and F gives a real, inverted, enlarged image beyond C.
questions.explanation: Apply the mirror formula and magnification with the sign convention.

questions.question: Light travels at 2.0 x 10^8 m/s in a transparent medium. Calculate the refractive index of the medium (take c = 3 x 10^8 m/s).
questions.answer:
Refractive index n = c/v = (3.0 x 10^8) / (2.0 x 10^8) = 1.5.
The medium has refractive index 1.5 (similar to ordinary glass). Since n > 1, light slows down in the medium and bends towards the normal when entering it from air.

questions.question: Explain why a ray of light passing through a rectangular glass slab emerges parallel to the incident ray. What is lateral displacement?
questions.answer:
On entering the slab (air to glass) the ray bends towards the normal; on leaving (glass to air) it bends away from the normal by the same amount, because the two faces are parallel. The two bendings are equal and opposite, so the emergent ray is PARALLEL to the incident ray.
However, the emergent ray is shifted sideways relative to the original direction. This sideways shift between the incident ray (extended) and the emergent ray is called the LATERAL DISPLACEMENT.
questions.explanation: Parallel faces cause equal and opposite bending; net shift = lateral displacement.

questions.question: A convex lens has a focal length of 20 cm. Calculate its power. State the unit and sign.
questions.answer:
f = 20 cm = 0.20 m.
Power P = 1/f = 1/0.20 = +5 D.
The power is +5 dioptres. It is POSITIVE because the lens is convex (converging). The unit of power is the dioptre (D), equal to 1 per metre.
questions.explanation: Apply P = 1/f with f in metres.

questions.question: Name the three common defects of vision. For each, state the cause and the type of corrective lens used.
questions.answer:
(1) MYOPIA (short-sightedness): distant objects appear blurred because the image forms in front of the retina (eyeball too long or lens too converging). Corrected with a CONCAVE (diverging) lens.
(2) HYPERMETROPIA (long-sightedness): near objects appear blurred because the image forms behind the retina (eyeball too short or lens too weak). Corrected with a CONVEX (converging) lens.
(3) PRESBYOPIA: an age-related defect in which the eye lens loses flexibility and the near point recedes, affecting near (and sometimes distant) vision. Corrected with BIFOCAL lenses (concave portion for distance, convex portion for near).
questions.explanation: Three defects, their causes and the corrective lens for each.

questions.question: What is dispersion of light? Write the order of colours obtained when white light passes through a prism.
questions.answer:
Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its seven component colours when it passes through a prism, because different colours travel at slightly different speeds in glass and are bent by different amounts (violet most, red least).
Order of colours (the spectrum) is VIBGYOR: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red.

questions.question: Why is the sky blue and why does the Sun appear reddish at sunrise and sunset?
questions.answer:
Both are due to SCATTERING of sunlight by air molecules, which scatter shorter (blue) wavelengths much more than longer (red) ones.
Blue sky: air molecules scatter the blue part of sunlight in all directions, so the sky looks blue.
Red Sun at sunrise/sunset: sunlight then travels a long slanting path through the atmosphere, so most of the blue light is scattered away before reaching us, leaving mainly the red and orange light - making the Sun and surrounding sky appear reddish.

questions.question: The blue colour of the sky is caused by the scattering of light.
The perpendicular drawn to a surface at the point of incidence is called the ____.
The apparent left-right reversal of an image in a plane mirror is called ____.
The centre of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror is called the ____.
A concave mirror of radius of curvature 30 cm has focal length ____ cm.
The mirror formula is 1/v + 1/u = ____.
For mirrors, magnification m = ____.
The refractive index n equals c divided by ____.
questions.explanation: n = c/v, v = speed in medium.

questions.question: After passing through a glass slab the emergent ray is ____ to the incident ray.
The lens formula is 1/v - 1/u = ____.
The power of a lens of focal length 1 m is ____ dioptre.
The least distance of distinct vision for a normal eye is about ____ cm.
The image formed on the retina of the eye is real and ____.
Myopia is corrected by using a ____ lens.
The order of colours in the spectrum of white light is ____.
The scattering of light by colloidal particles is called the ____ effect.
State the two laws of reflection of light.
questions.answer:
Law 1: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (i = r).
Law 2: The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

questions.question: What is meant by lateral inversion? Give an example.
questions.answer: Lateral inversion is the apparent swapping of the left and right sides of an image formed by a plane mirror. For example, your right hand appears as the left hand of your image, and the word AMBULANCE is written reversed on the front of the vehicle so that it reads correctly in a driver's rear-view mirror.

questions.question: List the properties of the image formed by a plane mirror.
questions.answer: (1) Virtual and erect (cannot be caught on a screen, upright). (2) Same size as the object. (3) As far behind the mirror as the object is in front. (4) Laterally inverted (left and right appear swapped).

questions.question: Define pole, centre of curvature and principal focus of a spherical mirror.
questions.answer:
Pole (P): the centre point of the mirror's reflecting surface.
Centre of curvature (C): the centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part.
Principal focus (F): the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis meet (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex) after reflection.

questions.question: The radius of curvature of a concave mirror is 24 cm. Find its focal length.
questions.answer: f = R/2 = 24/2 = 12 cm. The focal length of the concave mirror is 12 cm.

questions.question: Why is a convex mirror used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
questions.answer: A convex mirror always forms an erect, diminished (smaller) image and provides a wide field of view, so the driver can see a large area of traffic behind in a small mirror. The erect image is also easy to interpret. These advantages outweigh the fact that distances appear smaller than they really are.

questions.question: State two uses of a concave mirror.
questions.answer: (1) As a reflector in torches, vehicle headlights and search-lights (the bulb at the focus gives a strong parallel beam). (2) As a shaving or make-up mirror, giving an enlarged erect image when the face is within the focus. (Also: solar cookers/furnaces and by dentists.)

questions.question: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and magnification.
questions.answer:
u = -15 cm, f = -10 cm. Using 1/v + 1/u = 1/f:
1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/10 + 1/15 = -3/30 + 2/30 = -1/30.
So v = -30 cm (real image, 30 cm in front of the mirror).
Magnification m = -v/u = -(-30)/(-15) = -2 (real, inverted, twice the size).

questions.question: A convex mirror of focal length 12 cm forms an image of an object placed 24 cm in front of it. Find the image distance.
questions.answer:
For a convex mirror, f = +12 cm; u = -24 cm. Using 1/v + 1/u = 1/f:
1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/12 + 1/24 = 2/24 + 1/24 = 3/24 = 1/8.
So v = +8 cm. The image is 8 cm behind the mirror - virtual, erect and diminished.

questions.question: State the New Cartesian sign convention for spherical mirrors.
questions.answer: All distances are measured from the pole. Distances measured along the direction of the incident light are positive; distances against it are negative. Heights above the principal axis are positive, below are negative. Hence a real object's distance u is negative, and a concave mirror's f and R are negative while a convex mirror's are positive.

questions.question: For a concave mirror, describe the image when the object is (i) beyond C, (ii) at C, (iii) between F and the pole.
questions.answer:
(i) Object beyond C: image between F and C - real, inverted, diminished.
(ii) Object at C: image at C - real, inverted, same size as the object.
(iii) Object between F and the pole: image behind the mirror - virtual, erect, enlarged (the shaving-mirror case).
questions.explanation: Three image cases for a concave mirror.

questions.question: What is refraction of light? Why does it occur?
questions.answer: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium into another. It occurs because the speed of light is different in different media; the change in speed at the boundary causes the ray to change direction (bend), except when it strikes along the normal.

questions.question: State the laws of refraction of light.
questions.answer:
Law 1: The incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
Law 2 (Snell's law): For a given pair of media, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant: sin i / sin r = n (the refractive index).

questions.question: The speed of light in glass is 2 x 10^8 m/s. Find the refractive index of glass (c = 3 x 10^8 m/s).
questions.answer: n = c/v = (3 x 10^8) / (2 x 10^8) = 1.5. The refractive index of the glass is 1.5.

questions.question: Draw-in-words the path of light through a rectangular glass slab and explain lateral displacement.
questions.answer: Light entering the slab from air bends towards the normal; on leaving the slab it bends away from the normal by an equal amount because the two faces are parallel. So the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways. This perpendicular sideways shift between the original direction and the emergent ray is the lateral displacement.

questions.question: Why does a ray of light not bend when it falls normally (i = 0) on a surface?
questions.answer: When light strikes a surface along the normal, the angle of incidence is 0. By Snell's law sin r is also 0, so the angle of refraction is 0 - the ray continues straight through without bending, although its speed changes inside the new medium.

questions.question: Distinguish between a convex lens and a concave lens.
questions.answer: A convex (converging) lens is thicker at the middle than at the edges and brings parallel rays to a real focus. A concave (diverging) lens is thinner at the middle than at the edges and spreads parallel rays so they appear to come from a virtual focus. Convex lens has positive focal length/power; concave has negative.

questions.question: Write the lens formula and the formula for magnification produced by a lens.
questions.answer:
Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, where v is image distance, u is object distance and f is focal length.
Magnification: m = h'/h = v/u, where h' is image height and h is object height.

questions.question: A convex lens has a focal length of 25 cm. Find its power.
questions.answer: f = 25 cm = 0.25 m. P = 1/f = 1/0.25 = +4 D. The power is +4 dioptres (positive, because it is a converging lens).

questions.question: A concave lens has a power of -2.5 D. Find its focal length.
questions.answer: P = 1/f, so f = 1/P = 1/(-2.5) = -0.4 m = -40 cm. The focal length is -40 cm; the negative sign confirms it is a diverging (concave) lens.

questions.question: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Find the image distance and magnification.
questions.answer:
u = -30 cm, f = +20 cm. Using 1/v - 1/u = 1/f:
1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 + (-1/30) = 3/60 - 2/60 = 1/60.
So v = +60 cm (real image on the other side).
Magnification m = v/u = 60/(-30) = -2 (real, inverted, twice the size).

questions.question: What is the power of a lens? State its unit and sign convention.
questions.answer: The power of a lens is its ability to converge or diverge light, defined as P = 1/f, with f in metres. Its unit is the dioptre (D), where 1 D = 1 per metre. A convex (converging) lens has positive power; a concave (diverging) lens has negative power.

questions.question: Name the main parts of the human eye and state the function of each: cornea, iris, pupil, retina.
questions.answer:
Cornea: the transparent front layer where most bending of light occurs.
Iris: the coloured ring that controls the size of the pupil.
Pupil: the central opening that admits light (widens in dim light, narrows in bright light).
Retina: the light-sensitive screen at the back where the real, inverted image forms.

questions.question: What is accommodation of the eye?
questions.answer: Accommodation is the ability of the eye to adjust the focal length of its flexible eye lens (by the action of the ciliary muscles) so that objects at different distances are focused sharply on the retina. The lens becomes more curved (shorter focal length) for near objects and flatter for distant objects.

questions.question: Describe the image formed on the retina of the eye.
questions.answer: The cornea and eye lens together form a real, inverted and diminished image of the object on the retina. The retina sends the signal through the optic nerve to the brain, which interprets the image as upright.

questions.question: What is myopia? State its cause and how it is corrected.
questions.answer: Myopia (short-sightedness) is a defect in which a person can see nearby objects clearly but distant objects appear blurred. Cause: the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina because the eyeball is too long or the eye lens is too converging (short focal length). Correction: a concave (diverging) lens of suitable power diverges the incoming rays so the image is pushed back onto the retina.

questions.question: What is hypermetropia? State its cause and correction.
questions.answer: Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) is a defect in which a person can see distant objects clearly but nearby objects appear blurred. Cause: the image of a near object forms behind the retina because the eyeball is too short or the eye lens is too weak (long focal length). Correction: a convex (converging) lens of suitable power converges the rays so the image forms on the retina.

questions.question: What is presbyopia and how is it corrected?
questions.answer: Presbyopia is an age-related defect in which the eye lens gradually loses its flexibility and the ciliary muscles weaken, so the near point recedes and the eye cannot accommodate for near vision. Often both near and distant vision are affected. It is corrected using bifocal lenses, which have a concave portion (upper) for distant vision and a convex portion (lower) for near vision.

questions.question: What is dispersion of light? Name the colours of the spectrum in order.
questions.answer: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its seven component colours when it passes through a prism, because different colours bend by different amounts. The order of colours is VIBGYOR: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red.

questions.question: Explain why the sky appears blue and why the Sun appears red at sunset.
questions.answer: Both are due to scattering of sunlight by air molecules, which scatter shorter (blue) wavelengths far more than longer (red) ones. Blue sky: scattered blue light from all directions reaches our eyes, so the sky looks blue. Red Sun at sunset: sunlight travels a long slanting path through the atmosphere, so most of the blue is scattered away, leaving mainly red and orange light to reach us - making the Sun look reddish.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A student stands 2 m in front of a large plane mirror and observes her image.

(i) Is the image real or virtual?
(ii) How far behind the mirror is the image?
(iii) What is the size of the image compared with the student?
(iv) If she raises her right hand, which hand does the image appear to raise?
questions.answer:
(i) The image is VIRTUAL (it cannot be caught on a screen) and erect.
(ii) The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front - 2 m behind the mirror.
(iii) The image is the SAME SIZE as the student.
(iv) Because of lateral inversion, the image appears to raise its LEFT hand.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 40 cm.

(i) What is its focal length?
(ii) Where must a bulb be placed to get a parallel beam (as in a torch)?
(iii) Name one everyday device that uses such a concave mirror.
(iv) Is the focal length positive or negative by the sign convention?
questions.answer:
(i) f = R/2 = 40/2 = 20 cm.
(ii) The bulb must be placed at the principal focus (20 cm from the pole); rays then emerge parallel to the axis.
(iii) A torch, vehicle headlight or search-light reflector (also a shaving mirror is concave).
(iv) By the New Cartesian sign convention, a concave mirror's focal length is NEGATIVE (f = -20 cm).
questions.explanation: Concave mirror: f = R/2, uses, sign.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

An object 4 cm tall is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm.

(i) Find the image distance v.
(ii) Find the magnification m.
(iii) Find the height of the image.
(iv) State the nature of the image.
questions.answer:
u = -30 cm, f = -20 cm.
(i) 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/20 + 1/30 = -3/60 + 2/60 = -1/60, so v = -60 cm.
(ii) m = -v/u = -(-60)/(-30) = -2.
(iii) Image height h' = m x h = -2 x 4 = -8 cm (8 cm tall, inverted).
(iv) The image is real, inverted and enlarged (twice the object size), formed 60 cm in front of the mirror.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The refractive index of water is 1.33 and that of diamond is 2.42. (Take c = 3 x 10^8 m/s.)

(i) In which medium does light travel faster?
(ii) Calculate the speed of light in water.
(iii) Which medium bends light more?
(iv) State Snell's law.
questions.answer:
(i) Light travels faster in water (lower refractive index means higher speed, since n = c/v).
(ii) v = c/n = (3 x 10^8)/1.33 = 2.26 x 10^8 m/s (approximately).
(iii) Diamond bends light more (higher refractive index = more bending).
(iv) Snell's law: for a given pair of media, sin i / sin r = constant = refractive index n.

(i) Find the image distance v.
(ii) Find the magnification.

(iv) Calculate the power of the lens.

Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two thin lenses, a convex of focal length 20 cm and a concave of focal length 25 cm, are placed in contact.

(i) Find the power of the convex lens.
(ii) Find the power of the concave lens.
(iii) Find the net power of the combination.
(iv) Is the combination converging or diverging?
questions.answer:
(i) Convex: f = +0.20 m, P1 = +5 D.
(ii) Concave: f = -0.25 m, P2 = -4 D.
(iii) Net power P = P1 + P2 = 5 + (-4) = +1 D.
(iv) The net power is positive (+1 D), so the combination acts as a converging (convex) lens.
questions.explanation: Powers add for lenses in contact.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The human eye works like a camera, forming an image on a screen at the back.

(i) Name the screen on which the image forms.
(ii) What is the nature of the image formed there?
(iii) Which part adjusts the focal length of the eye lens?
(iv) What is the least distance of distinct vision for a normal eye?
questions.answer:
(i) The retina.
(ii) The image is real, inverted and diminished.
(iii) The ciliary muscles adjust the eye lens (this process is accommodation).
(iv) About 25 cm.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A student finds she cannot read the blackboard from the back of the class but can read her book clearly.

(i) Name the defect of vision she has.
(ii) Where does the image of a distant object form in her eye?
(iii) Which type of lens corrects this defect?
(iv) State one possible cause of the defect.
questions.answer:
(i) Myopia (short-sightedness).
(ii) The image of a distant object forms in front of the retina.
(iii) A concave (diverging) lens of suitable power.
(iv) The eyeball is too long, or the eye lens is too converging (focal length too short).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

An elderly man needs one pair of glasses to read and finds distant objects also slightly blurred.

(i) Name the age-related defect involved.
(ii) Why does it occur?
(iii) What type of lens (single) is used for the near-vision difficulty alone?
(iv) What kind of lens solves both near and distant problems at once?
questions.answer:
(i) Presbyopia.
(ii) With age the eye lens loses flexibility and the ciliary muscles weaken, so the eye cannot accommodate and the near point recedes.
(iii) For the near-vision difficulty alone, a convex (converging) lens is used.
(iv) Bifocal lenses (a concave portion for distant vision and a convex portion for near vision) solve both at once.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

When white light passes through a glass prism, a band of seven colours appears on a screen.

(i) What is this phenomenon called?
(ii) Write the order of the colours.
(iii) Which colour deviates the most and which the least?
(iv) Name a natural phenomenon that is an example of this.
questions.answer:
(i) Dispersion of light.
(ii) VIBGYOR: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red.
(iii) Violet deviates the most; red deviates the least.
(iv) A rainbow, formed when sunlight is dispersed by water droplets in the air.
